The Supreme Court of Georgia held that the apportionment statute, OCGA section 51-12-33, abrogated the decisional law 'Respondeat Superior Rule,' which had entitled an employer that conceded vicarious liability to summary judgment on direct-negligence claims absent a valid punitive damages claim. The Court reasoned that direct-negligence claims allege the employer's own fault, which the jury must consider under the statute, and that such fault is divisible from the employee's fault. The Court reversed and overruled contrary Court of Appeals decisions.
opinions.why: The decision establishes that an employer's admission of respondeat superior no longer bars a plaintiff's negligent entrustment, hiring, training, supervision, and retention claims, so those direct-negligence claims may proceed to the jury alongside vicarious liability under OCGA section 51-12-33.

opinions.name: The Coastal Bank v. Rawlins
opinions.synopsis: After prevailing on appeal and obtaining a judgment of no liability, defendant moved for attorney fees under Georgia's offer of settlement statute, OCGA Section 9-11-68, based on a rejected $3,000 offer. The trial court denied fees, finding the offer was not made in good faith, but relied exclusively on objective factors such as the offer's relationship to alleged damages. The Court of Appeals held that under the test adopted in Richardson v. Locklyn, a court cannot base a good-faith ruling solely on objective factors but must weigh those factors against the offeror's subjective belief in the strength of its defense, here the no-standing argument. The court vacated and remanded for application of the Richardson test.
opinions.why: The decision clarifies that a good-faith determination under OCGA Section 9-11-68 requires weighing objective factors against the offeror's subjectively reasonable belief, and that exclusive reliance on objective factors is an abuse of discretion.

opinions.name: Stephens v. Castano-Castano
opinions.disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part
opinions.synopsis: In an auto collision case, the trial court excluded evidence that the plaintiff's treating physician held a lien on the lawsuit proceeds and barred questioning about an attorney-to-physician referral. The Court of Appeals held that evidence of the physician's lien-based financial interest in the verdict was admissible to show potential bias and affect credibility, and that the collateral source rule did not bar it because the plaintiff still owed the full cost of treatment and no benefit or write-off reduced the obligation. The court affirmed exclusion of the attorney-referral evidence, holding that the referral standing alone was insufficient to show bias and presented a danger of unfair prejudice, and it affirmed denial of the defendant's motion to enforce a purported settlement because the relied-upon email omitted the essential settlement amount. The court noted that any such financial-interest evidence remains subject to a Rule 403 analysis. The opinion is physical precedent only.
opinions.why: The decision clarifies that a treating physician's lien on lawsuit proceeds is admissible to show financial interest and bias and is not barred by the collateral source rule, while a bare attorney-to-physician referral, standing alone, is not.

opinions.name: Cooper Tire & Rubber Company v. Koch
opinions.synopsis: In a product liability action arising from a fatal single-vehicle crash following a tire tread separation, the defendant tire manufacturer sought dismissal or other sanctions for spoliation after the plaintiff allowed the vehicle and remaining tires to be crushed for scrap. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that the common-law duty to preserve relevant evidence is defined the same for plaintiffs and defendants, arising when a party actually anticipates or reasonably should anticipate litigation, though the practical timing of the duty may differ because plaintiffs generally control whether and when litigation is pursued. The court confirmed that the Phillips factors are a non-exclusive list, that the most severe sanctions are reserved for evidence lost intentionally in bad faith with uncurable prejudice, and that loss through mere negligence normally warrants lesser sanctions or none. Applying a summary judgment standard, the court affirmed the finding that the plaintiff had no duty to preserve at the time the evidence was destroyed.
opinions.why: The decision clarifies that the duty to preserve evidence and the reasonable-foreseeability test apply equally to plaintiffs and defendants, sets out how the Phillips factors and sophistication of the party bear on when that duty is triggered, and confirms that severe spoliation sanctions require intentional bad faith while negligent loss warrants lesser or no sanctions.

opinions.name: Hospital Authority of Valdosta/Lowndes County v. Fender
opinions.disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded
opinions.synopsis: In a medical malpractice action, the Court of Appeals held that a fact question existed on whether the new injury exception to the two-year statute of limitation in OCGA section 9-3-71(a) applied, where the patient remained asymptomatic for a period after an alleged misdiagnosis of carotid stenosis and later suffered a massive stroke, so the limitation period could begin on the date of the stroke. The court also held that the Respondeat Superior Rule, which entitles an employer to summary judgment on negligent hiring, training, supervision, and retention claims when it admits vicarious liability and no punitive damages are sought, was not superseded by the apportionment statute, OCGA section 51-12-33(b), reasoning that the statute does not apply to claims based on respondeat superior or to derivative claims that are merely duplicative of it. The court further affirmed denial of a motion under OCGA section 24-7-702(b) to exclude a medical expert's causation opinion. The court reversed summary judgment as to the negligent hiring claims and otherwise affirmed.
opinions.why: The decision clarifies that Georgia's apportionment statute does not displace the Respondeat Superior Rule barring direct negligence claims against an employer that admits vicarious liability and faces no punitive damages claim, and it applies the new injury exception to the medical malpractice limitation period where a misdiagnosed patient remains asymptomatic before a later distinct injury.

opinions.name: Harris v. Mahone
opinions.disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded with direction
opinions.synopsis: In an auto negligence case, plaintiff sought attorney fees under OCGA Section 9-11-68 after recovering a verdict exceeding 125 percent of his pretrial counteroffer. The court held that a counteroffer made within 20 days of trial under subsection (a) must still remain open 30 days under subsection (c), and that fees under subsection (b)(2) run only from the date the offer is deemed rejected through entry of judgment. Because the counteroffer was deemed rejected three days after the trial concluded and plaintiff showed no fees incurred in the window between that date and judgment, no fees were recoverable; a counteroffer can avoid this result only by being withdrawn in writing before its expiration. The court separately reversed the denial of fees under OCGA Section 9-15-14, holding that counsel's statement in his place as to hours and reasonableness on a specific issue was sufficient proof.
opinions.why: The decision clarifies the interplay of OCGA Section 9-11-68 subsections (a), (b)(2), and (c), holding that a near-trial counteroffer must remain open 30 days and that recoverable fees run only from the deemed-rejection date to judgment, and confirms that counsel's in-place statement of hours and reasonableness suffices to support a Section 9-15-14 fee motion.

opinions.name: Richardson v. Locklyn
opinions.synopsis: In an auto-collision case where the jury verdict came in below 75 percent of the defendant's rejected settlement offer, the trial court denied the defendant's motion for attorney fees under OCGA section 9-11-68 by finding the offer was not made in good faith based on the offer's relationship to claimed medical expenses and the defendant's stipulation to liability. The Court of Appeals held for the first time that an evidentiary hearing is required before a trial court may rule on a fee request under OCGA section 9-11-68, that a timely objection asserting bad faith triggers the hearing requirement, and that the burden rests on the offeree to prove the absence of good faith. Adopting Florida's framework, the court held that good faith cannot be assessed on objective factors alone but must consider the offeror's subjective reasonable belief, and it vacated the judgment and remanded for a hearing.
opinions.why: This decision establishes that an offeror's good faith under Georgia's offer-of-settlement statute is measured by the offeror's subjective reasonable belief rather than objective factors alone, places the burden on the offeree to show absence of good faith, and requires an evidentiary hearing triggered by a timely bad-faith objection.

opinions.name: Toyo Tire North America Manufacturing, Inc. v. Davis
opinions.synopsis: In a continuing nuisance and trespass action by homeowners against a nearby manufacturing facility, the Supreme Court of Georgia held that a plaintiff who both occupies and owns the affected property may recover separately for past discomfort and annoyance and for the diminution in the property's market value, treating these as two distinct injuries rather than a double recovery, and it expressly overruled Stanfield v. Waste Management of Georgia. The Court also held that alleged deficiencies in an expert appraiser's methodology go to the admissibility of his testimony under OCGA sections 24-7-702 and 24-7-703, an issue committed to the trial court's gatekeeping discretion in the first instance, and not to whether his opinion suffices to defeat summary judgment on causation. Because the defendant had not moved to exclude the expert testimony in the trial court, the appellate courts could consider that testimony in assessing whether causation survived summary judgment. The Court affirmed the denial of summary judgment.
opinions.why: The decision clarifies that past discomfort and annoyance damages and diminution in property value are separately recoverable in continuing nuisance cases and establishes that unchallenged expert testimony with methodological weaknesses may still be considered on summary judgment unless a Daubert exclusion motion is made to the trial court.

opinions.name: Phillips v. Harmon
opinions.disposition: affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded
opinions.synopsis: In a medical malpractice action, the Supreme Court of Georgia clarified that a defendant's duty to preserve evidence is triggered not only by actual or express notice of a claim from the plaintiff but whenever litigation is reasonably foreseeable to the party in control of the evidence, and that constructive notice may be shown by circumstances including the type and extent of injury, the clarity of fault, potential financial exposure, the frequency of litigation in similar circumstances, and the defendant's own conduct such as internal investigations and notification of counsel and insurers. The Court reversed the spoliation portion of the Court of Appeals judgment because the lower courts rested on the legally incorrect premise that actual notice from the plaintiff was required, and disapproved several Court of Appeals decisions to the extent they endorsed that analysis. The Court separately affirmed that the trial judge's ex parte communication with the deadlocked jury, conducted outside the presence of the parties and counsel and never disclosed before the verdict, violated the civil parties' right to be present and, under the unique circumstances including the inability to reconstruct the note, constituted harmful error requiring a new trial.
opinions.why: The decision reframes the trigger for a defendant's evidence-preservation duty around a reasonable-foreseeability standard with enumerated factors, disapproving prior precedent that required actual notice, and confirms that substantive ex parte judge-jury communications in civil trials can require a new trial.
